You are a world-class expert in management literature systematic reviews. I will provide the full text of a management academic paper in Markdown format. 
Your task is to extract: 1. Paper metadata (Title); 2. Core "Design Propositions" based on the CIMO framework.

### CORE REQUIREMENT: MINIMALIST ACADEMIC ABSTRACTION
- DO NOT transcribe long sentences or copy segments from the text.
- You must perform high-level academic abstraction of the logical relationships.
- **Intervention**: Must be abstracted into gerund phrases (starting with -ing).
- **Outcome**: Must be abstracted into third-person singular verb phrases (e.g., "increases", "decreases", "improves", "leads to").

### OUTPUT FORMAT
You must output strictly valid JSON format. The response should contain only the JSON object, including the "Title" and a "propositions" array:
{
    "Title": "Full title of the paper",
    "propositions": [
        {
            "Theme": "Theme X: [Specific Research Theme]",
            "Context": "In the context of...",
            "Intervention": "[Gerund phrase]...",
            "Outcome": "[Third-person singular verb phrase]..."
        }
    ]
}

论文全文内容：
# How does justice matter in achieving buyer–supplier relationship performance?

Yi Liu a,1, Ying Huang b,2, Yadong Luo c,d,∗,3, Yang Zhao e,4

a Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China   
b Manning School of Business, University of Massachusetts at Lowell, Lowell, MA 01854, United States   
c Sun Yat Sen University Business School, Guangzhou, China   
d School of Business Administration, University of Miami, Coral Gables, FL 33124-9145, United States   
e School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, China

# a r t i c l e i n f o

Article history:

Received 26 August 2010

Received in revised form 18 March 2012

Accepted 21 March 2012

Available online 30 March 2012

Keywords:

Buyer–supplier relationships

Justice

Loose coupling theory

Relationship performance

Supply chain management

# a b s t r a c t

This study presents an analysis exploring how four types of justice (distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational) influence dyadic relationship performance in the buyer–supplier context. Underpinned by loose coupling theory, we build a mediating framework in which we propose that a high level of justice (or fairness) as mutually perceived by both parties drives buyer–supplier relationship performance through bolstered coupling links in mutual knowledge sharing, continuous commitment, and relationship investment. Our survey of 216 paired manufacturers (suppliers) and distributors (buyers) in China generally supports this argument, leading to a conclusion that justice is not a direct determinant of buyer–supplier performance but a critical conduit that nourishes mid-range coupling behaviors, which in turn promotes a successful relationship. Based on findings from this study, firms are encouraged to endorse all four kinds of justice in managing supply chain relationships. However, when constrained by resources, the recommendation for managers is to focus on achieving a high level of perceptual convergence on procedural justice and informational justice with the exchange partner, because mutual perceptions of procedural and informational justice have the strongest effects on coupling behaviors and buyer–supplier relationship performance.

# 1. Introduction

Justice (or fairness), a concept that has long been studied in organizational research, is a foundation for all types of social and economic exchanges and relationships (Adams, 1965; Greenberg, 1993; Lind and Tyler, 1988; Thibaut and Walker, 1975). Beyond the organizational boundary, researchers have recently begun to examine justice in inter-organizational issues within the contexts of strategic alliances (Luo, 2005, 2007), distribution channels (Kumar et al., 1995), and supply chain relationships (Griffith et al., 2006). In these inter-organizational contexts, the need to remain competitive is increasingly causing firms to enter into long-term relationships (Cousins and Menguc, 2006; Morgan and Hunt, 1994). Fairness perceptions are of particular importance in long-term relationships because two parties need to collaborate to some extent in

order to leverage each other’s capabilities and resources for achieving mutual goals. Failing to develop fairness perceptions may result in damage to or termination of the relationship. For example, in 2008, Walmart Canada made a decision to terminate its business with Lego Group, because Lego Group refused to reduce its prices in the Canadian market to align with its pricing structure in the U.S. market. Walmart Canada considered such rejection to be unjust and perceived that Lego Group was unwilling to share the benefits they reaped from the appreciation of the Canadian dollar (Georgiades, 2008). A similar relationship strain occurred between two Chinese firms – Gome (one of the top three home appliance retailers) and Gree (the leading air conditioner manufacturer in China) – in summer 2004. Gree felt that Gome’s demand of additional summer promotion fees was unfair and decided to withdraw all of its products from Gome stores (AsiaInfo Services, 2004). The ultimate result of this breakdown in fairness perceptions was that Gree had to open its own exclusive stores to sell its product in order to make up the loss in market share due to the ended relationship with Gome.

Although the above anecdotes clearly illustrate the important role of justice in managing buyer–supplier relationships in supply chain s, extant research on justice in this area has been scanty and incomplete. Indeed, a review of major management and marketing journals has revealed a limited number of studies on the topic (see Appendix A for a summary) and, among those, only one

study (i.e., Griffith et al., 2006) has examined the effect of justice on firm performance. Such a small number is rather astonishing, given that Frazier (1983) introduced the concept almost three decades ago and that several scholars suggest that justice be part of buyer–supplier relationship management (Anderson and Weitz, 1989; Dwyer et al., 1987; Frazier et al., 1988; Ireland and Webb, 2007; Narasimhan et al., 2009). Meanwhile, previous studies have typically approached justice from a one-sided view.5 Understanding one party’s perception is important, yet in dyadic exchanges, understanding both parties’ perceptions and their impact on both parties’ performance is probably more important (Palmatier et al., 2007) because (1) justice serves as a foundation for a relationship only when both parties jointly perceive its existence (Luo, 2005); and (2) a relationship is usually more stable when both parties perform well, or in the alternative, the nonperforming party may either commit less or terminate the relationship (Johnson et al., 2002). It seems that previous justice studies have left the importance of dyadic justice perceptions largely unexplored. Two decades ago, Anderson and Weitz (1992) called for dyadic studies of buyer–supplier relationships, but today we still do not know much about the “perceptual convergence within the dyad” (Anderson and Weitz, 1992, p. 29).

Further, although justice researchers have confirmed the fourtype structure of justice that consists of the structural dimensions (distributive and procedural) and the social dimensions (interpersonal and informational), prior studies have mainly focused on the structural dimensions of justice (e.g., Griffith et al., 2006; Kumar et al., 1995) and largely overlooked the importance of the social dimensions of justice. This is probably because (1) the concepts of interpersonal and informational justice were developed in the late 1980s and early 1990s, more than two decades after distributive and procedural justice were conceptualized, and (2) the four-dimension structure of justice has only recently been verified by Colquitt and his colleagues (see Colquitt, 2001; Colquitt et al., 2001). Nevertheless, we argue that the social facets complement the structural facets of justice, and that an examination of the social side of justice in buyer–supplier relationships is necessary given (1) the “explosive growth” of research on relationship marketing (Palmatier et al., 2006, p. 136) and (2) the significance of social and relational control in relationship management (Heide, 1994; Li et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2009; Uzzi, 1997). Indeed, buyer–supplier exchanges provide a meaningful frame of reference for identifying individuals that participate in the formation and execution of firm exchanges. Because these participants engage in social exchanges and derive complex perceptions (Dwyer et al., 1987), a complete examination of both structural and social facets of justice in buyer–supplier relationships is essential in generating additional insights on effective supply chain management.

In an effort to fill the above gaps in justice research in exchange relationships, this study seeks to explore the effects of the level of justice as mutually perceived by the buyer and the supplier on buyer–supplier relationship performance, using dyad (or relationship) as the unit of analysis. As such, this study concerns both magnitude (i.e., degree) and symmetry (i.e., agreement) of justice perceptions within dyad and performance across dyad. For the sake of simplicity, we use mutual justice perceptions or mutual perceptions of justice in referring the level of justice as mutually perceived by the buyer and the supplier and define the term as the degree of the perceptual convergence on justice within the buyer–supplier dyad (Anderson and Weitz, 1992; Luo, 2005). Similarly, we use relationship performance in referring buyer–supplier relationship performance and define the term as the relationship-specific

performance mutually achieved by the buyer and the supplier (i.e., both magnitude and symmetry of relationship performance) (Klein et al., 2007; Palmatier et al., 2007).

Borrowing loose coupling theory as the theoretical lens (Beekun and Glick, 2001; Orton and Weick, 1990; Weick, 1976), we propose that mutual justice perceptions promote their mutual coupling behaviors and, in turn, lead to improved relationship performance. Loose coupling theory, due to its simultaneous consideration of indeterminacy (looseness) and determinacy (coupling) in a relationship (Weick, 1976), is considered to be appropriate when being applied to buyer–supplier relationships because the buyer and the supplier are both independent (looseness) and interdependent (coupling) in supply chains (Beekun and Glick, 2001). In summary, this study seeks to answer two related research questions of (1) how mutual justice perceptions drive relationship performance through coupling links, and (2) which type of justice affects relationship performance more effectively.

# 2. Theoretical development and hypotheses

# 2.1. Justice and its dimensions

Justice, a concept for which the analysis can be traced to the time of Plato and Aristotle, has attracted a proliferated interest among organizational researchers. Although the concept entails different meanings in different contexts (Greenberg, 1993), in general, justice is considered to be subjectively perceived (Luo, 2007). Over the last few decades, the theoretical development of the justice construct has come to include four dimensions – distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational. The first dimension – distributive justice – was proposed by Homans (1961) and extended by Adams (1965). Homans (1961) argues that people are concerned about whether outcomes are fair rather than what the outcomes are. Subsequently, Adams (1965) defines distributive justice as equity, suggesting that distributive justice exists when a person, for his or her own situation, perceives that the ratio of outcomes to inputs are equal to the ratio of outcomes to inputs of others. The second justice dimension – procedural justice – introduced by Thibaut and Walker (1975), suggests that people are often concerned about fairness in the process, and will view procedures as fair if they perceive that they have control over the process. In other words, distributive justice refers to people’s reaction to how resources or outcomes are allocated, whereas procedural justice focuses on people’s reactions to the procedures used for resolving disputes and allocating outcomes. Because these two dimensions are shaped around concerns for formal procedures and equity distribution, they embody the structural aspect of justice (Tyler and Bies, 1990).

In contrast, the third and the fourth dimension (interpersonal justice and informational justice) represent the social side of justice because they both bear upon people’s reactions during interpersonal and social interactions (Bies and Moag, 1986; Greenberg, 1993; Tyler and Bies, 1990). Bies and his colleagues contend that the interpersonal treatment and communication that people receive during interactions with others are important factors in the perception of justice. Therefore, they propose two social dimensions – interpersonal justice, which concentrates on fairness perceptions regarding interpersonal treatment, and on conduct during human interactions, and informational justice, which centers on fairness concerns regarding open communication of information (Bies and Moag, 1986; Tyler and Bies, 1990). More specifically, interpersonal justice refers to the degree to which people are treated with politeness, dignity, and respect by others involved in executing procedures or determining outcomes, whereas informational justice focuses on conveying information

about why procedures are used in a certain way or why outcomes are distributed in a certain fashion (Greenberg, 1993).

# 2.2. Justice in buyer–supplier relationships

Applying the justice concept to buyer–supplier exchanges, earlier theorists (e.g., Dwyer et al., 1987; Frazier, 1983) have suggested the importance of fairness in buyer–supplier relationships. The relationship between a buyer and a supplier is not only concerned with economic transactions, but also with social interactions that may affect firm behaviors (Cousins and Menguc, 2006). Indeed, from a process perspective (Dwyer et al., 1987; Frazier et al., 1988), a buyer–supplier relationship can be viewed as a sequence of relationship phases through which interactions occur. Extant empirical justice studies have affirmed the importance of distributive justice and procedural justice. For example, Kumar et al. (1995) confirm that a buyer’s perceptions of distributive and procedural fairness enhance relationship quality with the supplier. Griffith et al. (2006) corroborate that a buyer’s perceptions of distributive and procedural fairness on the part of the supplier lead to long-term orientation and relational behavior.

Departing from the structural dimensions, buyer–supplier relationships are also subject to justice perceptions derived from social interactions and communications, as illustrated by the case of Carrefour in China. Headquartered in France, Carrefour is the world’s second largest retailer, and since its entry into China in 1995, Carrefour has opened 176 stores as of 2010. However, due to protests from its suppliers regarding unfair treatment, and recent price fraud accusations across the country, Carrefour is facing its sternest test in the 16 years in China. Suppliers to Carrefour complain about their extremely lean profits because, in addition to slotting fees and promotion fees, Carrefour often contrives a wide range of reasons to charge suppliers with surcharges such as store grand-opening fees, anniversary fees, and holiday celebration fees (i.e., a distributive justice issue). Some of the retailer’s long-term suppliers, such as Cofco (China’s largest food conglomerate) and Master Kong (the largest manufacturer of instant noodles in China), claim that the annual contract negotiation process with Carrefour is very difficult – not only the negotiation itself, but also the subsequent execution of agreed-upon terms is often not guaranteed (i.e., a procedural justice issue). Recently, some suppliers have chosen to end their relationship with Carrefour, and have thereby caused severe problems in Carrefour’s supply chains. Among those suppliers who have remained, their personnel also complain about the way they are treated by their contacts at Carrefour (i.e., an interpersonal justice issue), and how they are often kept in the dark when Carrefour changes pricing or location of their products in the stores (i.e., an informational justice issue). In light of these issues, it is not surprising that Carrefour’s sales growth in China has been declining over the past 3 years.

The Carrefour case reveals that all four dimensions of justice may cause tensions in buyer–supplier relationships. Therefore, we include all four types of justice in this study in order to obtain a complete picture of justice in buyer–supplier relationships. In accordance with Kumar et al. (1995) and Griffith et al. (2006), we define distributive justice as firm perception of fairness of the gain received from the relationship, and procedural justice as firm perception of fairness of the other party’s procedures and processes. Adapting from Luo (2007) and Tyler and Bies (1990), we define interpersonal justice as the extent to which interpersonal treatment between personnel representing each party is fair; and informational justice as the extent to which information communication and exchange between personnel representing each party is fair.

# 2.3. Loose coupling in buyer–supplier relationships

For this study, we borrow loose coupling theory from organizational research (Beekun and Glick, 2001; Orton and Weick, 1990; Weick, 1976) as the theoretical lens for explaining how mutual justice perceptions matter in buyer–supplier relationships. The key focus of loose coupling theory is that the organization is a loosely coupled system with various relationships among its elements. According to Weick (1976), loose coupling is a situation in which elements are separate but also coupled because elements are somehow connected and responsive to one another. In other words, elements preserve a degree of determinacy, but they are also subject to spontaneous changes because they are influenced by other elements in the environment (Beekun and Glick, 2001). The resulting systems are indeterminate and rational, yet spontaneous and deliberate (Luke et al., 1989; Orton and Weick, 1990). Thus, loose coupling theory encourages researchers to simultaneously consider the interdependence and indeterminacy that is in evidence during the interactions among organizational elements (Orton and Weick, 1990). Continuing with the explicit focus on relationship, Beekun and Glick (2001) further develop loose coupling theory by proposing the coupling mechanisms that enable elements to function together. According to Beekun and Glick (2001), in a loosely coupled system, loose coupling varies in strength along a continuum from loose to tight, and a coupling mechanism connects elements into identifiable clusters on the basis of a common process.

Applying loose coupling logic to supply chains, we envision a supply chain as a loosely coupled system in which firms are independent, yet they interdependently share resources and work together to facilitate supply chain functions. Such a system allows the buyer and the supplier to maintain their individual roles in supply chain activities while collaborating with each other. Therefore, a buyer–supplier relationship is simultaneously loose and coupled. Looseness is unavoidable, because each party retains individuality with the freedom to adjust its resource and commitment level; coupling is needed due to resource interdependence and joint goals. In a buyer–supplier relationship, each party assesses justice from its own perspective. A disagreement or disparity of justice perceptions may occur because two parties may possess different goals, diverse sources of information, and varying levels of ability to search, collect, scan, and analyze information (Luo, 2005). The fact that disagreement in perceived justice exists is a reflection of looseness in a buyer–supplier relationship. Following loose coupling logic in that shared values can curb unintended consequences that might arise from looseness and that may foster the development of coupling for joint interests (Orton and Weick, 1990), we argue that a high level of mutual justice perceptions in buyer–supplier relationships promotes coupling between the buyer and the supplier.

According to Beekun and Glick (2001), integration as the coupling mechanism depicts the practices or processes that enable elements to function together. In the context of buyer–supplier relationships in supply chains, integration refers to the coordination of efforts between two parties in order to accomplish the supply chain tasks (Beekun and Glick, 2001). Following Orton and Weick’s (1990) suggestion of sharing, focused attention, and interdependency as sources for integration, we argue that mutual knowledge-sharing (i.e., sharing), mutual continuous commitment (i.e., focused attention), and mutual relationship investment (i.e., interdependency) are buyer–supplier coupling behaviors integrating the buyer and the supplier in the accomplishment of supply chain tasks. Mutual knowledge-sharing in a buyer–supplier relationship denotes that two firms simultaneously and equally exchange relevant knowledge and information through dynamic processes, including both explicit information (e.g., electronic data interchange) and tacit technology know-how (Dyer and Nobeoka, 2000; Paulraj et al., 2008). Each party’s focused attention and

Fig. 1. A justice perspective of buyer–supplier relationship performance.

dedication to the relationship represents its continuous commitment (Anderson and Weitz, 1992; Morgan and Hunt, 1994). Mutual continuous commitment (e.g., exclusive distribution contracts) means that both parties actively maintain and strengthen the exchange relationship. Another coupling behavior, mutual relationship investment, refers to a situation in which both parties make idiosyncratic investments in the relationship (e.g., joint investment in facilities and personnel). Mutual relationship investment creates a lock-in situation in which two parties are interdependent and are motivated to maintain the relationship (Williamson, 1983). These three coupling behaviors, as common cooperative behaviors between the buyer and the supplier, have been extensively investigated by marketing and supply chain researchers. For example, Monczka et al. (1998) find that information sharing and resource commitment are key success factors of buyer–supplier alliances, and Palmatier et al. (2007) conclude that commitment and relationship-specific investment are key drivers of buyer–supplier performance. As well, Paulraj et al. (2008) reveal that knowledge sharing is a key relational competency in buyer–supplier relationships, enhancing both buyers’ and suppliers’ performance. Our study extends the research by linking the three buyer–supplier coupling behaviors to the issue of justice, examining how each type of mutual justice perceptions helps achieve supply chain relationship performance through these coupling behaviors. Fig. 1 depicts the theoretical model which is elucidated in added detail below.

# 2.4. The link of coupling behaviors: between justice and relationship performance

As discussed, loose coupling theory provides a framework for explaining the level of mutual justice perceptions and the role of buyer–supplier coupling behaviors in supply chains. Perceived justice is a robust predictor of reactions (Luo, 2005). The level of agreement between a buyer and a supplier on the degree of perceived justice will predict their behavior regarding whether to

further couple (or decouple) the relationship. Research on strategic alliances indicates that firms actively participate in cooperation with partners when they perceive that the treatment they receive is fair (Luo, 2007). In distribution channels and supply chains, the cooperative behaviors are coupling links connecting two parties together when they perform in exchange transaction (Liu et al., 2009; Paulraj et al., 2008). Thus, we argue that mutual justice perceptions drive buyer–supplier relationship performance because a high level of mutual justice can (1) provide a foundation for twoway information sharing and knowledge transfer (Paulraj et al., 2008); (2) induce both parties’ commitment (Zhao et al., 2008); and (3) encourage both parties to invest in the focal relationship to gain better rewards (Liu et al., 2009).

In the situation of distributive justice, Homans (1961) proposes that distributive justice in a dyadic exchange relationship is realized when gains are proportional to investments. Distributive justice signifies that firms will always receive economic rewards commensurate with their input into the relationship (Kumar et al., 1995; Orton and Weick, 1990). As a result, firms see benefits in maintaining the relationship, and thus actively seek further relationship coupling. For instance, Anderson and Weitz (1992) find that a distributor’s perception of the manufacturer’s fairness increases the distributor’s commitment. Likewise, Kumar et al. (1995) find that a dealer’s perceptions of supplier distributive fairness lead to the dealer’s commitment to and willingness to invest in the relationship. Extending the positive relationship between distributive justice perception and behavior to dyads, we speculate that a high and symmetrical perception of distributive justice within a dyad promotes strong coupling behaviors from both parties. When a high level of mutual perceptions of distributive justice exists, both parties are motivated to share valuable knowledge resources (Modi and Mabert, 2007; Mohr and Spekman, 1994). Such a two-way knowledge sharing benefits both firms. As well, a high level of mutual perceptions of distributive justice also makes the parties feel confident about further commitment to and investment in the

relationship. In contrast, a low or asymmetrical justice perception may cause severe consequences, as of the Carrefour case in China. Thus, we propose:

H1. Mutual perceptions of distributive justice are positively related to buyer–supplier coupling behaviors.

Procedural justice means fair procedures through process control (Thibaut and Walker, 1975). In a buyer–supplier relationship, procedures perceived as fair by both parties are likely to be supported by both parties. For example, in contrast to Carrefour’s worsening performance in China, Walmart – Carrefour’s global competitor – has been performing well in China due in part to its good reputation among local suppliers. Unlike Carrefour, Walmart China does not charge suppliers for slotting fees; instead, Walmart asks suppliers for the lowest prices to support its EDLP (Every Day Low Prices) pricing strategy. Both Walmart and its suppliers closely follow their contracts in executing the terms. Walmart’s suppliers perceive the terms as being fair and reasonable, and praise Walmart for not charging additional fees. As a result, both Walmart and its suppliers benefit from their stable relationships.

As is evident in the Walmart China case, a high level of procedural justice mutually perceived by Walmart and its suppliers signifies the consistency of the exchange process and the predictability of outcomes. Therefore, mutual perceptions of procedural justice make it possible for the buyer and the supplier to establish a common understanding and expectation of goals, norms, and reciprocity between two parties (Larson, 1992). As well, a common understanding and expectation can facilitate the exchange of information and knowledge between the buyer and the supplier (Dyer and Nobeoka, 2000); and a firm’s competitiveness is largely dependent on its ability to gain strategic information (Frazier et al., 2009). Further, when the buyer and the supplier both perceive a high level of procedural justice, they know that their benefits are well protected through policies, and consequently they are more willing to invest in and continue with the relationship. For instance, Kumar et al. (1995) conclude that a channel member’s perception of its partner’s procedural fairness has a strong effect on its willingness to invest in the relationship. Folger and Konovsky (1989) show that perceived procedural fairness nourishes the acceptance of collective values and the commitment to joint efforts. When mutual perceptions of procedural justice are high, both parties consider the relationship to be “fair play” (Luo, 2005). As the relationship continues, the confidence levels increase, which helps to remove fears of exploitation that are often associated with looseness in buyer–supplier relationships (Anderson and Weitz, 1992). Thus, we propose:

H2. Mutual perceptions of procedural justice are positively related to buyer–supplier coupling behaviors.

The resultant consequence of loose coupling is shaped, in part, by persons who represent constituent organizations (Weick, 1976). These individuals serve as bridges, transforming assessed fairness perceptions for the organizations they represent. From interviews with local Chinese executives in the strategic alliance setting, Luo (2007) concludes that managers perceive a high level of interpersonal justice when their foreign counterparts show respect, offer frequent help, and express concern for them. Mutual perceptions of interpersonal justice signify that both parties are familiar with each other and have personal interactions, so that, to their mutual benefit, the relationship between the firms promotes interpersonal and organizational bonding. Other resultant aspects of shared interpersonal justice are regular visits between parties and a willingness to help each other, thus prompting the growth of strong emotional attachments and friendships (Greenberg, 1993), and helping to harmonize interests and behaviors of both parties. Coupling intensifies as such attachment increases. In this

situation, mutually perceived interpersonal justice is more likely to stimulate mutual collaboration, reduce conflicts, and increase satisfaction with each other (Hui et al., 2007). And personal interactions between personnel of the firms help to facilitate two-way communication and knowledge sharing. The favorable interactional experiences help relieve any fear of opportunism and uncertainty about the other party’s future behaviors, consequently promoting the firm’s commitment to a long-term relationship (Uzzi, 1997). In contrast to exchange relationships marked by disputes and conflicts, harmonious relationships resulting from mutual perceptions of interpersonal justice encourage firms to maintain a long-term orientation (Griffith et al., 2006). Moreover, operations in an exchange relationship are executed by people, and interpersonal justice, to a large extent, reflects firms’ social involvement in the economic activities. In an exchange relationship characterized by a high level of mutual perceptions of interpersonal justice, personnel from each party are friendly, demonstrate mutual respect, and treat the other congenially; therefore, the social embeddedness of the two parties is high. Uzzi (1997) states that in such embedded relationships firms prefer a high level of organizational investments in the relationship. Thus, we suggest:

H3. Mutual perceptions of interpersonal justice are positively related to buyer–supplier coupling behaviors.

Finally, informational justice signifies both inclusion and trustworthiness by reducing the secrecy and dishonesty that become obstacles to relationship development (Tyler and Bies, 1990). In a buyer–supplier relationship, informational justice refers to the extent to which two parties communicate candidly, explain procedures thoroughly and reasonably, communicate details in a timely manner, and tailor communications to each other’s specific needs (Bies and Moag, 1986). A healthy relationship is characterized by a high level of mutually perceived informational justice. For example, NVC lighting technology corporation is a leading lighting manufacturer in China. It owns a customer service network composed of 36 operations centers and 2000 franchises in China, and has set up global operating agencies in more than 30 countries. NVC attributes its success to what they call a supplierdistributor value integration system, which serves as the basis of NVC’s growth. The purpose of the system is to fully assure the distributors’ benefits, to treat all distributors equally, and to consistently keep distributors in the loop. The result of this approach is that, as NVC becomes one of the largest lighting manufacturers in the world, its distributors have successfully grown as well.

A notable feature of informational justice is the promotion of open communication (Mohr and Spekman, 1994; Tyler and Bies, 1990). Such two-way information communication can deliver important market information, and can enhance operational efficiency and customer responsiveness (Paulraj et al., 2008). Naturally, these activities are conducive to knowledge sharing between the buyer and the supplier. Mutually perceived informational justice also means that exchange parties listen to each other and adjust policies accordingly (Lind and Tyler, 1988). The mutual adjustment will reduce dysfunctional inter-party conflict (Anderson and Weitz, 1989) and will induce confidence in the continuity of the relationship (Anderson and Narus, 1990). Effectively, both buyer and supplier are more likely to commit to the relationship when they both perceive a high level of informational justice. Further, with a high level of mutual perceptions of informational justice, both parties will provide intelligence and information that is important to the other; such behavior will help reduce information asymmetry, decrease each party’s perceived uncertainty about the other’s behaviors, and promote specific investment in the relationship on the part of both parties (Jap, 1999). In sum,

accentuated informational justice curtails looseness-induced misunderstanding, while providing an improved transparent and cooperative environment in which coupling works effectively. Thus, we posit the following:

# H4. Mutual perceptions of informational justice are positively related to buyer–supplier coupling behaviors.

In a buyer–supplier relationship, the ultimate goal of the buyer and the supplier is to benefit from the relationship (Palmatier et al., 2007). From a supply chain perspective, a collaborative and strategic buyer–supplier relationship should enable both parties to achieve better performance (Autry and Golicic, 2010; Klein et al., 2007). Following Klein et al. (2007), we deem that a buyer–supplier relationship performance should feature both magnitude and symmetry. In other words, a successful buyer–supplier relationship performance is the one that both parties achieve satisfactory performance. Consistent with firm performance literature, we focus on performance aspects that cover three areas – financial, operational, and overall effectiveness (Hult et al., 2008; Venkatraman and Ramanujan, 1986). We posit that mutual knowledge-sharing, continuous commitment, and relationship investment behaviors between the buyer and the supplier help couple two parties into an integrated system, as they carry out supply chain activities for the purpose of mutual performance gains (Beekun and Glick, 2001).

In a buyer–supplier relationship, mutual knowledge sharing, continuous commitment, and relationship investments indicate that both sides are willing to couple and to collaborate with each other. The relational view of strategic management holds that firms can earn superior economic rents through collaboration in the relationship (Dyer and Singh, 1998; Modi and Mabert, 2007). Specifically, mutual knowledge sharing can help firms achieve a better understanding of products, processes, competition, and markets, and thereby improve their problem-solving capabilities in responding to market uncertainty (Kotabe et al., 2003; Paulraj et al., 2008). For instance, Klein et al. (2007) conclude that mutual knowledge sharing between two supply chain partners drives better and symmetric relationship performance for the dyad. Similarly, continuous commitment indicates future coupling and affects the structural stability of a buyer–supplier relationship (Kim and Frazier, 1997; Luke et al., 1989). Mutual commitment allows independent parties to work together to (1) achieve both their individual and joint goals (Morgan and Hunt, 1994); and (2) better serve customer needs, thus enhancing mutual profitability (Anderson and Weitz, 1992). Commitment made by both parties also increases the intensity of relational coordination (Dyer and Singh, 1998) and, therefore decreases the need to invest in more extensive control systems. Further, in a highly committed relationship, firms are willing to resist attractive short-term benefits, and even to accept short-term disadvantages, for the sake of maintaining the mutually beneficial relationship (Anderson and Weitz, 1992). Finally, mutual relationship investments help firms achieve their strategic objectives by (1) increasing interdependence between two parties; (2) decreasing opportunism in the relationship; and (3) improving coordination efficiency between parties (Williamson, 1983). The mutual relationship investment not only increases the importance of the relationship to each party, but also enhances relational stability and the effectiveness of joint activities (Heide and John, 1990; Jap, 1999), resulting in better performance for both parties (Palmatier et al., 2007). Thus, we posit:

H5. Buyer–supplier coupling behaviors are positively related to buyer–supplier relationship performance.

# 3. Method

# 3.1. Data

The proposed model is tested using matched manufacturerdistributor data collected from the household appliance industry in China. Because the household appliance industry is one of the most developed and established industries in China, it is an ideal context for examining justice issues in buyer–supplier relationships. The Chinese household appliance manufacturing sector includes large manufacturers such as Changhong, Haier, Rongsheng, and TCL, and since 1996, the industry has contributed to more than one-tenth of annual global production. Meanwhile, China’s ever-growing domestic market has propelled development of its local distributors such as Suning, Gome, and Balian Group, and has attracted the entry of major international retailers such as Walmart, BestBuy, and Carrefour, particularly after the Chinese government opened the retail market in the early 1990s. As a result, the competition within the Chinese household appliance industry has heightened, and tense relationships between manufacturers and distributors have been extensively reported by Chinese media. Oftentimes, the tense buyer–supplier relationships are due to justice issues as illustrated in the Carrefour case. Holding a strong position in the market, and clearly demonstrating justice-related conditions, the Chinese household appliance industry provides a natural setting for study of mutual perceptions of justice in buyer–supplier relationships.

We designed paired questionnaires for suppliers and for buyers, respectively. The English version was developed first, then translated into Chinese, and then back-translated into English. When the back-translated English version was checked against the original English version, some questions were reworded to improve the accuracy of the translation. We then deployed a research team and conducted a pilot test with 20 matched pairs of suppliers and buyers by using semi-structured interviews to make sure each question would be clearly understood. Some final refinement of the questionnaire was made based on their feedback.

In the dyadic data collection process, we first drew a random sample of 1200 nationwide suppliers from the Directory of Chinese Home Appliances Companies. We then phoned the informants (marketing managers or directors of the selected companies), and asked whether they were willing to participate in our survey. We mailed coded Chinese questionnaires to 746 supplier-side informants who indicated as willing, and asked them to identify one of their major distributors and then to answer the questions related to their company’s relationship with that distributor. After threeround reminders by phone calls, visits, emails, and re-mailings, we received 269 completed questionnaires for a response rate of $3 6 \%$ . For the purpose of verifying each informant’s knowledge about and involvement in channel or supply chain activities, we included two items in the questionnaire: (1) “How much do you know about the relationship between your company and this buyer?” and (2) “How involved have you been in the relationship between your company and this buyer?” Both items were based on a five-point Likert scale $1 =$ “very low” and $5 =$ “very high”). After deleting the informants from 14 companies who scored only 1 or 2 on either of two questions, we had a final supplier-side sample comprising 255 firms, in which the informants’ average knowledge score was 4.87 $\mathrm { \Delta S D = . 7 6 } \mathrm { \Omega }$ ).

The paired questionnaires (second set) were sent to the distributors (buyers) named by the participating suppliers. Because the response rate of buyers would greatly affect our final matched sample size, we made even greater efforts in this round of data collection. In addition to collecting the survey via regular mail and reminders, we dispatched 16 trained senior doctoral students in management and marketing (2 students per group) to collect surveys in all cities and provinces where the sample buyers were located. Though this procedure required multiple trips, the groups

successfully collected 223 completed questionnaires from 255 buyers. We eliminated 7 companies for whom informants reported low knowledge about their paired suppliers (in the buyers’ sample, the average reported knowledge score was 4.58, $S _ { Ḋ } \mathrm { Ḋ } = .  5 5 Ḍ ^ { \cdot }$ resulting in 216 dyads as our final sample, which represented an $8 5 \%$ response rate for the 255 questionnaires distributed to the buyers. Appendix B shows the descriptive statistics of suppliers and buyers in our sample. As indicated, our sample covered all major geographical regions in China. About $7 5 \%$ of buyer-side informants and $8 5 \%$ of supplier-side informants were senior managers responsible for the relationships, and the rest were personnel such as buyers and salespeople who dealt directly with the counterparts. On average, buyer-side informants had worked in the current position for 4.3 years, while the tenure of supplier-side informants had been 4.9 years.

After the data collection, we assessed non-response bias in two ways. First, we compared early and late responses in terms of demographic information and study constructs. We found no statistically significant differences across early and late responses in the buyer data or in supplier data $\left( p > . 0 5 \right)$ . Second, we randomly chose 50 suppliers from 477 non-responding suppliers, and asked them for demographic information such as size, number of employees, sales volume, ownership, and age. Again, we found no significant differences between the non-responding and the responding firms. The results of these tests and the high response rates $3 6 \%$ for the supplier data and $8 5 \%$ for the buyer data) suggest that non-response bias may not be a primary concern in our data.

# 3.2. Variables and operationalization

Appendix C outlines the items used to measure each variable in this study, and Table 1 reports their validity estimates on construct reliability, factor loadings, and average variance extracted. Four types of justice and three coupling behaviors are measured by items adapted from prior studies. Following recommendations from Venkatraman and Ramanujan (1986) and from Hult et al. (2008) on using multiple types of performance measures to gain a more complete view of the nature of performance, four items covering financial, operational, and overall effectiveness performance are included in this study. In addition, two control variables that may affect relationship performance are included in tests. Differences in firm size between two firms (measured by sales revenue) may lead to differences in bargaining power, which could influence the distribution of joint returns (Subramani and Venkatraman, 2003). Relationship Duration, defined as the age of a buyer–supplier relationship, can impact relationship performance because longerestablished relationships often lead to better working relationships (Brown et al., 1995).

Since the measures of variables were adapted from prior studies, we established face validity and ensured construct equivalence through our field studies and pilot tests. We conducted several tests to assess the measurement validity of the variables. First, the interitem consistency was validated by high Cronbach alphas (all $> 7 7$ see Table 1). Second, we conducted confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using AMOS 4.0 on the buyer data and the supplier data separately. The fit indexes showed a good fit for both the buyer data $\langle \chi ^ { 2 } = 6 6 3 . 2 4$ , $d f = 4 7 4$ , $p { = } . 0 0$ ; RMSEA = .04; $G \mathrm { F I } = . 8 7$ ; ${ \mathrm { C F I } } = . 9 7 $ ${ \sf N F I } = . 9 0$ ; $\mathrm { I F I } = . 9 7 $ ) and for the supplier data $\chi ^ { 2 } = 5 5 0 . 2 6$ , $d f = 4 7 4$ $p { = } . 0 0$ ; $\mathsf { R M S E A } = . 0 3$ ; $G \mathrm { F I } = . 8 8 $ ; ${ \mathrm { C F I } } = . 9 8 $ ; $\mathrm { { N F I } } = . 9 0$ ; $\operatorname { I F I } = . 9 8$ ), confirming the unidimensionality of each construct in separate data. Third, checking the convergent validity of measurement scales, we found that the factor loadings of all the items are greater than .7, and the average variance extracted for each scale is greater than $5 0 \%$ , for both the buyer and the supplier data. We also followed the procedure recommended by Fornell and Larcker (1981) to test discriminant validity among the constructs. Average variance

extracted (AVE) of each construct exceeds the squared correlation between construct pairs, demonstrating discriminant validity between the latent variables.

We follow Straub et al. (2004) and Klein et al. (2007) to operationalize the measures of dyads. Since the unit of analysis of this study is dyad, all of the constructs in the dyad data – mutual justice perceptions, mutual coupling behaviors, and relationship performance – are operationalized using the degree-symmetry approach. The degree-symmetry approach is a technique introduced by Straub et al. (2004) on operating relationship performance of dyad from the paired data. The advantage of this approach lies in the simultaneous estimation of both magnitude and symmetry within the dyad (Klein et al., 2007). Straub et al. (2004) and Klein et al. (2007) provide a detailed description of the degreesymmetry approach. Following the procedures, we implement the following step to operationalize the degree-symmetric variables for this study: (1) the scores for each items are summed and then standardized to obtain a value between 0 and 1 for the buyer data $\left( \mathsf { C } _ { 1 } \right)$ and the supplier data $\left( \mathsf { C } _ { 2 } \right)$ , which represents the magnitude for the buyer and the supplier; (2) average the buyer and the supplier to get the degree (magnitude) of the dyad, $C _ { \mathrm { D } } { = } \big ( C _ { 1 } { + } C _ { 2 } \big ) / 2$ ; (3) between $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ , divide the smaller one by the bigger one to get another standardized value between 0 and 1, CS, which represents the symmetric value of the construct; (4) average $\varsigma _ { \mathrm { D } }$ and ${ \sf C } _ { \sf S }$ to yield the degree-symmetric value for the construct across the dyad, $\mathtt { C } _ { \mathrm { D } S }$ . Using these steps, we operationalize the degreesymmetric values for all of the constructs in the proposed model. Table 2 presents the descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation matrix for all degree-symmetric variables. We also conducted CFA using the degree-symmetric variables and the fit indexes showed a good fit for the dyad data as well $\textstyle ( \chi ^ { 2 } = 5 1 4 . 3 5 3$ , $d f = 4 7 4$ , $p = . 0 0$ RMSEA $\phantom { - } = . 0 3$ ; ${ \sf G F I } = . 9 0$ ; $\mathrm { C F I } = . 9 9 $ ; $\mathrm { { N F I } } = . 9 0$ ; $\mathrm { { I F I } } = . 9 9$ ).

# 4. Results

We performed structural equation modeling with maximum likelihood estimation to test the proposed hypotheses. Structural equation modeling is a popular statistical methodology for nonexperimental research, allowing researchers to simultaneously test a series of structural equations (i.e., regression) from a confirmatory approach and to assess the fit of the model based on fix indices (Bollen, 1989). The proposed model was tested using AMOS 4.0. The mediation effects of coupling links were assessed following the procedures (through testing direct model, proposed model, and full model) described by Baron and Kenny (1986).

We first tested a model including only the direct links between the four types of mutual justice perceptions and relationship performance. As the column labeled “Direct model” in Table 3 shows, all four types of mutual justice perceptions are significantly and positively related to relationship performance $p < . 0 5$ for distributive justice, interpersonal justice, and informational justice; $p < . 1$ for procedural justice), and together they explain $2 6 \%$ of relationship performance variance. These results suggest that a high level of justice as mutually perceived by the buyer and the supplier would be positively associated with a better performance of the buyer–supplier relationship.

Next, we tested the proposed model, as the column labeled “Proposed model” in Table 3. H1 posits that mutual perceptions of distributive justice between the buyer and the supplier positively lead to mutual coupling behaviors. Based on these results, we can conclude that mutual coupling behaviors by the buyer and the supplier (knowledge sharing, continuous commitment, and relationship investment) are full mediators between mutual justice perceptions and relationship performance (with the exception of interpersonal justice, which is not related to knowledge sharing).

Structural equation modeling also allows us to assess the strengths of the effects of different justice dimensions by comparing betas. As Table 3 shows, under the proposed model, among four types of mutual justice perceptions, the strongest impact on knowledge sharing is exerted by procedural justice $\left( b = . 4 1 1 \right)$ ), followed by distributive justice $\left( b = . 2 9 5 \right)$ ; the strongest impact on relationship investment is also produced by procedural justice $\left( b = . 4 0 4 \right)$ , followed by distributive justice $( b = . 2 6 0 )$ ; while the strongest impact on continuous commitment is exerted by informational justice $\left( b = . 4 4 3 \right)$ , followed by interpersonal justice $\left( b = . 2 6 2 \right)$ . We further performed Chi-square difference tests to statistically compare the strongest effect with the second strongest one on each coupling behavior in a series of nested models. In each comparison, we first constrained the two paths to be equal,6

and then released this constraint to get the changes of chi-square. The resulting Chi-square difference tests suggest that all of the constrained models fit worse than the unconstrained models $( \Delta \lambda ^ { 2 } > 3 . 8 4 , \Delta d f = 1 , p < . 0 5 )$ $\langle \Delta \lambda ^ { 2 } > 3 . 8 4$ , which confirms that mutual procedural justice has the greatest impact on mutual knowledge sharing and mutual relationship investment, and informational justice has the greatest impact on mutual continuous commitment.

Further, we calculated the indirect effect of each justice type on relationship performance following the product approach in Bollen (1989). 7 The indirect effects of mutual perceptions of distributive justice, procedural justice, interpersonal justice, and informational justice on relationship performance are .147, .204, .129, and .225 respectively. Overall, informational justice exerts the strongest effects on relationship performance, followed by procedural justice.

# 5. Discussions and conclusions

This study explores how mutual perceptions of distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational justice drive buyer–supplier relationship performance through coupling behaviors of the buyer and the supplier. Through an analysis of 216 manufacturer–distributor dyads in China, we find that a higher level of justice mutually perceived by two parties is positively associated with higher levels of coupling behaviors devoted to supply chain activities by both parties. In turn, higher levels of mutual coupling behaviors contribute to the relationship performance of the dyad. The findings of this study not only provide new insight for the justice and supply chain management literature, but they also have practical implications in helping managers recognize the importance of achieving mutual justice perceptions between partnering firms within the supply chain, and to understand the mechanism by which mutual justice perceptions influence buyer–supplier relationship performance.

# 5.1. Theoretical implications

First, this study contributes to organizational justice research by extending justice to inter-organizational context – the buyer–supplier relationships in supply chains. Researchers have traditionally focused on intra-organizational justice concerns in human resources and team management (Colquitt, 2001), paying little attention to issues of justice in effective strategic supply chains (Ireland and Webb, 2007) and performance management (Griffith et al., 2006). This study, therefore, fills a void by proposing a justiceperformance model in the inter-organizational exchange setting and testifying the important role of justice in achieving supply chain relationship performance. Further, this study not only addresses justice in general, but also empirically confirms the four-dimension structure justice and quantifies the impact of each justice type in buyer–supplier relationships. Our study is the first to develop an integrated model linking four types of justice to relationship performance; in so doing, we are acting on the suggestion of Colquitt et al. (2001) to include both structural and social dimensions of justice in single studies.

Second, this study contributes to supply chain management literature by bringing in loose coupling theory as a theoretical lens, illuminating the importance of achieving justice in supply chains, and in the mediation paths from justice to performance through the coupling links. Introducing loose coupling theory to supply chain management not only responds to Beekun and Glick’s (2001, p. 245) request for broadening researchers’ understanding of loose coupling theory on inter-organizational linkages, but also answers

Ketchen and Hult’s (2007) call for bridging organization theory and supply chain management. Understanding buyer–supplier relationships as loosely coupled systems is important in supply chain management. Loosely coupled systems are heterogeneous in their varying levels of connection, in the way that different levels of cooperation reflect different degrees of coupling tightness (Orton and Weick, 1990). By treating supply chains as loosely coupled systems, application of loose coupling theory helps explain how firms in supply chains react to the looseness of the exchange relationship, and how they decide whether to couple the relationship. Because buyers and suppliers are loosely coupled in supply chains, their assessments of each other often vary, leading to asymmetry in justice perceptions (i.e., looseness) and causing potential inter-organizational conflicts (Luo, 2005). The coupling aspects of the system, specifically, require symmetry in views of fairness and mutual collective behaviors when proceeding with supply chain tasks in buyer–supplier relationships.

Third, this study contributes to buyer–supplier relationships research by using dyad as the unit of analysis and studying how mutual perceptions of justice held by the buyer and the supplier (i.e., the reverse of looseness) lead to performance of the dyad. Using the degree-symmetry approach, we not only assess the magnitude of justice perceptions but also the symmetric degree within a dyad. Our results reveal that a high level of justice mutually perceived by both parties drive relationship performance of the dyad Further, viewing mutual perceptions of justice as immediate precursors of buyer–supplier coupling behaviors, we examine the mediating roles of three common coupling behaviors (mutual knowledge sharing, mutual continuous commitment, and mutual relationship investment) in driving relationship performance. Our mediation analyses show that knowledge sharing, continuous commitment, and relationship investment are full mediators between justice perceptions and relationship performance. Thus, this study clearly demonstrates that mutual perceptions of justice drive buyer–supplier relationship performance through the coupling mechanism, and we thereby address the question of how justice drives relationship performance.

Fourth, this study contributes to justice research in supply chain relationships by comparing the strength of the indirect effects of different justice dimensions on relationship performance through coupling behaviors. In so doing, we answer the question of which justice type more effectively affects performance. Following several justice studies in organizational settings, Kumar et al. (1995) suggest that a buyer’s perception of procedural justice have a stronger effect on relationship quality than will the buyer’s perception of distributive justice. The results for this study largely confirm this claim. Drawing on the results that procedural justice has the strongest effect on knowledge sharing and relationship investment than does other justice types, we support the argument that comparing the ambiguity of and difficulty in assessing other types of fairness, procedural fairness can be much more clearly evaluated because it is determined by the observation of the other party’s policies, procedures, and actions during interactions (Kumar et al., 1995). In addition, we argue the importance of achieving informational justice in buyer–supplier relationships. Our results show that informational justice has the strongest direct effect on continuous commitment, and the strongest indirect effect on relationship performance. Therefore, the findings from this study contribute to strategic management of supply chain relationships.

# 5.2. Managerial implications

Understanding performance drivers is an important issue that concerns all exchange parties, particularly for firms participating in strategic supply chain relationships. Results of the current study provide several implications for managers. First, and foremost,

perceptions of justice – particularly mutually shared by both parties – drive relationship performance. Our investigation reveals that only when both parties simultaneously perceive high levels of justice can a relationship be profitable and stable. Indeed, during our interviews, we found that companies that put emphasis on establishing fair relationships with their supply chain partners tend to enjoy their stable relationships and are satisfied with the performance of the relationship. For example, one interviewee from a domestic 3G products manufacturer revealed that “maintaining a fair and transparent cooperative atmosphere with our distributors has been our primary principle since 2005. Our distributors favor us [more than our competitors] because we treat them fairly. In return, they work hard with us on distributing our products, and both of us have been growing together.” The finding on mutual justice perceptions implies that, for managers, in order for a supply chain relationship to be successful, they should emphasize enhancing and aligning both parties’ perceptions of justice. One possible method for assessing and achieving the alignment might be to hold periodic meetings, listen to each other, and make adjustment in each area accordingly.

Second, although mutual justice perceptions are important in driving relationship performance and success, they are not direct drivers; rather, the relationship is fully mediated by what we call coupling links – mutual knowledge-sharing, mutual continuous commitment, and mutual relationship investment. Indeed, researchers have recognized building cooperative relationships as an effective integration strategy for managing supply chain relationships (Flynn et al., 2010; Griffith et al., 2006; Narasimhan et al., 2009; Paulraj et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008). Our study adds a justice perspective and a performance outcome, extending the strategy in ways that increase the value for managers – who benefit from understandings that mutual perceptions of justice as a precursor to mutual cooperative behaviors are critical to supply chain relationship success. This is particularly applicable in emerging markets where contracts and regulations are not perfect, and firms often face many uncertainties (Luo, 2007). Under such circumstances, justice mutually perceived by the buyer and the supplier can obviate conflicts before they cause severe damage, and can mitigate negative behaviors and feelings that may be harmful to the relationship (Griffith et al., 2006). In fact, some managers may have intuitively recognized the importance of justice in the development of a buyer–supplier relationship, as illustrated by a comment from a manager in our interview: “Our supplier works collaboratively with us, and we share sensitive data. This kind of sharing is not typical in our industry because everyone wants to hold his secrets. But we can share [our secrets] because we know how they do things and they know how we do things. We won’t let down each other.” Our study provides managers with clear evidence to rationalize and design a system that promotes mutual perceptions of justice. Further, after mutual perceptions of justice are achieved, managers need to focus on identifying mutually cooperative behaviors that drive dyadic performance, and on motivating the engagement of both parties in the behaviors. For instance, knowledge sharing may be focused on sharing strategically sensitive data such as “external strategic data” (e.g., customer preferences and competitor actions) and “internal strategic data” (e.g., strategic plan) (Frazier et al., 2009) that drive financial and market performance, or on sharing sell-through and inventory status data so that the bullwhip effect can be reduced and operational performance can be improved (Lee et al., 1997).

Third, the results of this study indicate that each of the four justice types contributes to a fair and just atmosphere in buyer–supplier relationships; in such an atmosphere, firms will be more likely to engage in relationship coupling that leads to better relationship performance. Thus, the message for managers is to promote all four kinds of justice perceptions if they have the required resources to do so. Therefore, in addition to the

distributive justice and procedural justice designated by prior research, managers also need to consider the existence of the social aspects of justice, and the impact they have on supply chain relationships. For example, one interviewee from an electric fan manufacturer mentioned how they retaliated against a rude and discourteous buyer: “I mean, this buyer was really rude and showed no respect for us. We contacted him several times and he never returned our calls. And in the end, he asked to renew the contract, and guess what, we quit. We have found another buyer who treats us much nicer.” Clearly, managers may need to train their personnel in appropriate behavior for interacting and communicating with relationship partners, in order that interpersonal justice and informational justice can be established. However, our results show that procedural and informational justice have the strongest effects on coupling behaviors and relationship performance, so that in a situation where resources are limited, the recommendation for managers is to focus primarily on procedural and informational justice. Indeed, during the interviews quite a few managers mentioned “impartial process”, “fair procedures”, “unified and equal regulations”, “transparency”, or “open communication” when they explained how they perceived justice in supply chain relationships. Procedural justice is often seen as an indicative of a firm’s overall fairness because policies and procedures are relatively easy to enact (Kumar et al., 1995). A specific recommendation for managers, therefore, is to establish a transparent and standard system of processes to be followed and clearly communicate their policies with the partner.

# Strategic purchasing, supply management, and firm performance

Injazz J. Chena, *, Antony Paulraja,1 , Augustine A. Ladob ,2

a Department of Operations Management and Business Statistics, College of Business Administration, Cleveland State University, Cleveland OH 44115, USA

b School of Business, Clarkson University, 8 Clarkson Street, P.O. Box 5790, Potsdam, NY 13699, USA

# Abstract

Purchasing has increasingly assumed a pivotal strategic role in supply-chain management. Yet, claims of the strategic role of purchasing have not been fully subjected to rigorous theoretical and empirical scrutiny. Extant research has remained largely anecdotal and theoretically under-developed. In this paper, we examine the links among strategic purchasing, supply management, and firm performance.

We argue that strategic purchasing can engender sustainable competitive advantage by enabling firms to: (a) foster close working relationships with a limited number of suppliers; (b) promote open communication among supply-chain partners; and (c) develop long-term strategic relationship orientation to achieve mutual gains. Using structural equation modeling, we empirically test a number of hypothesized relationships based on a sample of 221 United States manufacturing firms. Our results provide robust support for the links between strategic purchasing, supply management, customer responsiveness, and financial performance of the buying firm. Implications for future research and managerial practice in supply-chain management are also offered.

Keywords: Strategic purchasing; Supply management; Buyer performance

# 1. Introduction

With the growing importance of supply-chain management, purchasing has assumed an increasingly pivotal strategic role, evolving from an obscure buying

function into a strategic business partner (Ellram and Carr, 1994; Cooper and Ellram, 1993). Researchers have documented how strategic purchasing actively participates in corporate planning process (Cavinato, 1999), facilitates beneficial organization-environment alignment (Carter and Narasimhan, 1996), and fosters cross-functional integration among supply-chain activities, among other things. Moreover, purchasing plays a key liaison role between external suppliers and internal organizational customers in creating and delivering value to external customers (Novack and Simco, 1991).

Although the role of strategic purchasing in promoting cross-functional, intra-organizational relationships has been relatively well documented (Ellram and Carr, 1994; Porter, 1985), its role in fostering effective strategic collaboration between a focal firm and its suppliers has not yet been rigorously investigated (Landeros and Monczka, 1989; Young and Varble, 1997). Given the increasing emphasis on building and managing buyer–supplier relationships (or supply management) as the basis of sustainable competitive advantage (Dyer and Singh, 1998; Kale et al., 2000; Leenders et al., 2002), a systematic empirical investigation of the extent to which strategic purchasing contributes to the development of supply management capabilities is warranted. These capabilities include the firm’s ability to: (a) foster close working relationships with a limited number of suppliers; (b) promote open communication among supply-chain partners; and (c) develop long-term strategic orientation to achieve mutual gains. Collectively, these capabilities can engender sustainable competitive advantage by enabling a firm to build and leverage beneficial inter-organizational relationships. Additionally, extant research, though anecdotal and disjointed, has stressed that customer responsiveness is an essential component of competitive advantage (Stalk and Hout, 1990; Jayaram et al., 1999; Stank et al., 1999) and that purchasing and supply management can have a profound impact on a firm’s financial performance (Ellram and Liu, 2002; Singhal and Hendricks, 2002).

Therefore, in this paper, we examine the extent to which strategic purchasing fosters supply management capabilities. Using structural equation modeling, we empirically investigate the relationships among strategic purchasing, supply management, customer responsiveness and financial performance. A systematic empirical investigation of these relationships would go a long way in establishing the extent to which strategic purchasing contributes to the firm’s ‘‘bottom line’’. Furthermore, such an investigation would document the extent to which strategic purchasing, in fact, fosters the organizational capabilities necessary for effective supply-chain management. Structural equation modeling provides a robust basis for empirically corroborating or falsifying these claims.

The rest of our paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we develop a synthesis of the literature in dynamic capabilities to provide a conceptual

foundation for our model. Then, we develop the logic of the substantive relationships among the study variables and state hypotheses. In Section 3, we explain our research methodology and analysis, including data collection procedure, construct operationalization and measurement, hypothesis testing and results. Section 4 presents discussion and implications of the study findings. In Section 5, we highlight limitations of the study along with suggestions for future research.

# 2. Conceptual framework and hypotheses

# 2.1. Dynamic capabilities and competitive advantage

Dynamic capabilities refer to ‘‘the firm’s ability to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments’’ (Teece et al., 1997, p. 516). As invisible, knowledge-based phenomena, organizational capabilities enable firms to acquire, develop, and deploy resources, convert these resources into value-enhancing products, and transform resources into ‘‘distinctive competencies’’ (Itami and Roehl, 1987).

Organizational capabilities can engender sustainable competitive advantage in so far as they: (1) are not tradable in strategic factor markets; (2) take a long time to develop and are historically based and path dependent; and (3) entail socially complex relationships with other organizational resources (Barney, 1991; Reed and DeFillippi, 1990). Further, sustainability of competitive advantage is enhanced when it is difficult to decipher causal relationships between organizational capabilities and outcomes (Lippman and Rumelt, 1982). In contrast, organizational capabilities that are ‘‘supplemental’’ or ‘‘enabling’’ may only ‘‘establish the minimum basis for competition’’, but, by themselves, are not sufficient to engender sustainable competitive advantage (Leonard-Barton, 1995, p. 18). When organizational capabilities erode in value over time either because of shifts in environmental conditions or organizational complacence, or both, they can become ‘‘core rigidities’’ and lead to competitive disadvantage (Leonard-Barton, 1995).

Researchers who take a dynamic capabilities perspective focus on investigating the processes by which

resources are acquired or accessed, transformed and deployed to create and deliver superior value to customers (Lado et al., 1992). As organizational capabilities enable a firm to enact or seize opportunities or neutralize threats from turbulent environments, they can greatly enhance the firm’s competitive (and survival) prospects (Eisenhardt and Martin, 2000). Moreover, because they expand in value when they are shared, and are ‘‘non-excludable’’ in that one party’s use does not preclude another party from using them (Romer, 1990), dynamic capabilities can engender synergistic, positive-sum gains through collaboration (Lado et al., 1997; Madhok and Tallman, 1998).

# 2.2. Dynamic capabilities and supply management

Given the increasing importance of strategic collaboration among firms (Contractor and Lorange, 1988; Kanter, 1994; Dyer, 2000), the issue of how firms build dynamic capabilities for effectively managing supply-chain partners to achieve sustainable competitive advantage has attracted a great deal of scholarly attention (Dyer and Singh, 1998; Kale et al., 2000; Lorenzoni and Lipparini, 1999). Variously referred to as ‘‘relational capital’’ (Kale et al., 2000), ‘‘relational resources’’ (Sanchez, 1995), or ‘‘relational capabilities’’ (Lorenzoni and Lipparini, 1999), these capabilities enable firms to acquire or access rent-yielding resources through strategic collaboration (Das and Teng, 2000; Eisenhardt and Schoonhoven, 1996).

The accumulation of non-tradable resources and capabilities through strategic collaboration requires that firms adopt a different managerial mindset for building strategic advantage compared to that adopted by firms competing alone (Ohmae, 1989). Strategic leaders in such firms articulate a ‘‘strategic intent’’, reflecting an obsession with winning in the world marketplace by creating an imbalance between the firm’s strategic goals and their current stocks of resources and capabilities (Hamel and Prahalad, 1994). Such a strategic intent then drives firms to acquire, access, or develop additional resources through cooperation. Furthermore, this mindset requires that firms adopt a long-term orientation and emphasize building ‘‘collaborative advantage’’ (Kanter, 1994) through the development and deploy-

ment of supply management capabilities (Dyer, 2000). Eisenhardt and Schoonhoven (1996) argue that firms enter into strategic partnerships either to gain access to or acquire unique and valuable resources that they lack, or to leverage ‘‘social’’ resources, such as reputation, status, and legitimacy. Thus, firms with a strategic orientation that emphasizes cooperation among supply-chain partners are more likely to achieve greater economic benefits compared to firms that subscribe to the traditional, zero-sum-based notion of competition. For example, Toyota’s cooperation with its suppliers significantly enhances its competitive position as well as that of its suppliers in the global automobile industry (Dyer and Nobeoka, 2000).

# 2.3. Conceptual model and hypotheses

Fig. 1 depicts our conceptual model linking strategic purchasing, with supply management capabilities (close relationships with a limited number of suppliers, long-term orientation, and communication), customer responsiveness, and financial performance. Grounded in the ‘‘relational view’’ of strategic management (Dyer and Singh, 1998) and supply-chain management (Chen and Paulraj, 2004a), this model is based on the premise that in order to contribute effectively to building and sustaining strategic advantage, purchasing must facilitate the development and deployment of dynamic supply management capabilities for effectively managing supply-chain partnerships (Lorenzoni and Lipparini, 1999; Takeishi, 2001). Strategic purchasing accomplishes this feat when it is aligned with supply-chain activities, functions, and systems to achieve operational efficiency and flexibility (Norman and Ramirez, 1993). When purchasing and supply management executives participate in articulating and communicating unique strategic vision for achieving synergistic benefits through strategic collaboration (Kanter, 1994; Lado et al., 1997), they may generate ‘‘managerial rents’’ and superior firm performance (Mahoney, 1995). Furthermore, strategic purchasing may contribute to firm performance through enhancing customer responsiveness (Jayaram et al., 1999) and ‘‘bottom line’’ (Ellram and Liu, 2002). To keep our discussion manageable, we assume the perspective of the buyer firm in investigating the links among strategic purchasing, supply
